stories.title: Multi-analytical study of the ancient Khan-Geum (韓錦) silk brocade excavated from the Taklamakan Desert
stories.description: This study employed a multi-analytical approach—accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), and X-ray diffraction (XRD)—to investigate the manufacturing technology and material characteristics of the Khan-Geum (韓錦) brocade excavated from the Taklamakan Desert. AMS radiocarbon dating places the brocade in the 1st–2nd century AD. FT-IR and XRD together identify a β-sheet-rich fibroin (crystallinity index ≈ 51%, above that of a modern reference silk measured under identical conditions), indicating that the disordered amorphous regions were preferentially lost while the ordered β-sheet core was retained—a selective, amorphous-first degradation rather than wholesale preservation or advanced breakdown. SEM and cross-sectional measurements reveal a bimodal distribution of fiber circularity and cross-sectional area, a variability that suggests a mixture of raw silk types rather than a single uniform stock, with partial degumming that preserved sericin as a cohesive sizing agent for untwisted yarns. Structural analysis classifies the textile as a quadruple warp-faced compound tabby of exceptionally high density (174 ends/cm, 24 picks/cm; warp-to-weft ratio 7.3:1). The divided-warp mechanism enabled five-color patterning within a four-layer matrix, indicating sophisticated heddle control. Triangular borders and localized lacquer residues reinforced the selvedge and protected the textile surface. These findings establish the Khan-Geum as a technological benchmark for early high-density warp-faced silk brocades. The integration of zoomorphic and cloud motifs, together with a woven inscription containing the ethnonym 韓 (Khan), suggests the use of a sophisticated multi-heddle and multi-treadle horizontal loom capable of producing highly detailed, non-linear patterns at extreme warp densities. Collectively, these findings indicate that the brocade was produced within a highly developed warp-faced weaving tradition of the eastern Silk Road, reflecting a refined synthesis of fiber selection, structural design, and symbolic expression.

stories.title: Product-based kinetic analysis reveals limitations of substrate depletion method for assessing bile salt hydrolase activity
stories.description: Bacterial bile salt hydrolases (BSH) catalyze the initial step in microbial bile acid transformation and play a key role in host-microbiome interactions. However, reliable ex vivo assessment of BSH activity, particularly its kinetic characterization, remains limited. Here, we developed an LC–MS-based assay to characterize BSH activity in murine cecal content and evaluated its performance in a model of cholestasis induced by 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine (DDC). Enzymatic activity was assessed using three major tauro-conjugated substrates: taurocholic (TCA), taurochenodeoxycholic (TCDCA), and taurodeoxycholic acid (TDCA). Product-based analysis revealed Michaelis–Menten-type kinetics for all substrates. Apparent Km values increased in the order TDCA < TCDCA < TCA, indicating decreasing substrate affinity, while maximal reaction rates followed the reverse trend (TCA < TCDCA < TDCA). In DDC-treated mice, BSH activity was reduced, as reflected by decreased apparent Vmax. In contrast, measurements performed at sub-Km concentrations were variable and did not consistently reflect the expected group-level differences. Similarly, substrate depletion approaches failed to distinguish between experimental groups. Among the tested substrates, TCDCA provided the most robust readout due to minimal endogenous background and clear differences at near-saturating concentrations. These findings highlight the importance of Vmax-oriented analysis and multi-concentration assessment for reliable evaluation of BSH activity.
